name: Hassan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Okay to start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, fire away. I've been thinking about this stuff a lot, so you might have to stop me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start with a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior dozer operator at an open-pit lithium mine, and I run the earthworks crew: two dozers, a grader and a big excavator. These days I spend about half my time running a dozer remotely from a cabin at the edge of the pit, with screens and joysticks, because we were one of the first sites to try it. The rest of the time I'm planning the push for the next bench, which is the next step down in the pit, with the mine planners. I like that it's half machine and half puzzle. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the endless meetings when something goes wrong with the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we got the useful bits and skipped the scary bits, which is a decent outcome. I'd probably post a little thread about how remote dozing is still the future, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes for me. I'd still be on the remote system, still pushing for more of it, still running the drone business on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the drone surveying business, maybe buy a second drone with a better camera and hire my cousin Faris on weekends. At the mine I'd push for the second remote dozer. Money's fine, I'd keep investing the surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a side business on the form. What is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fly survey drones for farmers and small building sites on my days off, mapping ground levels and stockpiles. I made more last month flying a drone over three farms than I did working two overtime shifts. It's small but it's growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I use one to process the drone images into maps, one to draft quotes for clients, and I ask one to check my push plans for the dozer. It's like a sharp assistant who never gets tired, though it doesn't know the pit like I do.

S0.say: He'd say the outcome is decent, with the useful bits kept and the scary bits skipped. He'd post a thread about remote dozing being the future regardless of AI.
S0.think: He thinks not much changes for him: he'd still run the remote system, push for more of it, and grow his weekend drone business.
S0.do: Grows the drone surveying business with a second drone and his cousin Faris working weekends. Pushes for a second remote dozer at the mine and keeps investing his surplus.
S0.quote: I made more last month flying a drone over three farms than I did working two overtime shifts.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan is energetic and already living partly in the automated future, splitting his time between a remote cabin and a weekend drone business. He uses AI daily and speaks of it as a tireless assistant. The side business is a meaningful second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but I'd say it kindly. The machines are going remote anyway, so get on the training early. That's what I'd say to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good for me. I'm already the remote guy, and if more machines go remote, I'm the one they need. The drone side would grow too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to run the remote operations cabin full-time and train the rest of the crew on it. I'd put more money into the drone business, maybe register it properly and get a contract with a local quarry. I'd keep a big cash buffer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, our grader operator, he's fifty-five and hates screens. I'd sit next to him for as many shifts as it takes, because he taught me how to read a slope by eye. But I'm not sure he'd want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine for the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. The mine pays well and the drone business is still small. I'd do both until the drone money matched half my wage, then think about it.

S1.say: He'd tell the crew to adapt early, kindly, since machines are going remote anyway and training early is the smart move.
S1.think: He sees it as good for him because he's already the remote operator they'll need, and his drone side business would grow too.
S1.do: Asks to run the remote operations cabin full-time and train the crew. Registers the drone business properly, chases a contract with a local quarry and keeps a big cash buffer.
S1.quote: I'd sit next to him for as many shifts as it takes, because he taught me how to read a slope by eye.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan is positioned to gain in this picture and says so plainly. His warmth shows towards Pete, the older grader operator who taught him, though he doubts Pete would want help. He's cautious enough to keep his main job while the side business grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's make it work. Governments need to move fast on income support. I'd say it without blaming anyone, because it's just happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my edge is gone. Remote operator, drone surveyor, both of those get done by AI with no human in two years. I've got money, but my plan was to keep moving one step ahead, and there's no step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at buying into equipment, maybe a share in a local contracting firm with autonomous machines, so I own something that earns. I'd move a chunk of savings into broad shares. And I'd turn the drone business into a fleet I manage rather than fly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm used to feeling ahead, and here I'm just in the crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your drone business is also something AI and robots could do. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. In two years a drone will fly itself, map the site and send the invoice. I'd need to own the drones, not fly them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd sell or buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my car and buy a cheaper one. Then put that money into a share of a machine fleet with my uncle's contracting firm. Owning is the only thing that makes sense if work disappears.

S2.say: He'd say it's here so people should make it work, and governments need to move fast on income support. He wouldn't blame anyone, because it's simply happening.
S2.think: He thinks his edge vanishes because AI will do both remote operating and drone surveying within two years, leaving no next step.
S2.do: Sells his car for a cheaper one and buys a share of an autonomous machine fleet in his uncle's contracting firm. Moves savings into broad shares and turns the drone business into a fleet he manages rather than flies.
S2.feel: Anxious, because he's used to being ahead and here he's just one of the crowd.
S2.quote: In two years a drone will fly itself, map the site and send the invoice. I'd need to own the drones, not fly them.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan's strategy shifts from staying ahead to owning machines. Two years is too short for his usual advantage, which is why he's anxious despite his savings. He doesn't blame anyone and treats the change as a fact to work around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's plan it. Training, investment in local businesses, that kind of thing. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to build something. I'd have the drone business big enough to automate, and I'd own part of a machine fleet before everyone else rushes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd turn the drone business into a proper company with three drones and an auto-processing setup. I'd start buying into the contracting firm in small chunks. I'd stay at the mine, because the wage pays for the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, busy way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm buying whatever's left. Five years, I'm buying before the rush, and that's the difference between owning a fleet and renting a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at the mine in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably until 2029 or so. Once the remote cabin is run by AI, I'd leave and run the business full-time.

S3.say: He'd say five years is time to plan, and he'd keep it practical. He'd talk about training and about investing in local businesses.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to build something: an automated drone business and a stake in a machine fleet bought before the rush.
S3.do: Turns the drone business into a proper company with three drones and automated processing in the first year. Buys into his uncle's contracting firm in small chunks and stays at the mine to fund it, leaving around 2029.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but in a busy, productive way.
S3.quote: Five years, I'm buying before the rush, and that's the difference between owning a fleet and renting a flat.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Hassan's plan is to buy ownership before others rush in. He sees the gap between owning and renting as the key divide after AGI. He'd keep his mine wage as long as it lasts to fund the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway. Use it to build things people own locally, not just wait for a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm in a strong spot. Business built, shares in a fleet, savings, all by thirty-seven. I'd be fine, and I think I could help my family be fine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same as five years, just slower and with less risk. Year one, register the drone company and do a business course at night. Year three, buy into the fleet. Stay at the mine until about year seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can see a path all the way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you do differently from the five-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less rushing. I'd also get a proper business qualification, because running a fleet is a different skill. With ten years, I could go from operator to owner without betting the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn how to run things, not just do them. And save early. My cousin Faris is nineteen, and he's already asking me how to start.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a decent runway to build locally owned businesses instead of waiting for a cheque.
S4.think: He thinks ten years leaves him in a strong spot by 37, with a business, a stake in a fleet and savings, and able to help his family.
S4.do: Registers the drone company and starts a night business course in year one, buys into the machine fleet around year three, and stays at the mine until about year seven.
S4.feel: Calm, because he can see a path all the way through.
S4.quote: With ten years, I could go from operator to owner without betting the house on it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Hassan follow his plan without risk, which is why he's calm. He shifts from operator to owner deliberately. He wants to pass on the habit of saving and running things to his younger cousin.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be scrambling instead of planning. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses to buy their own machines, so it's not just the big companies owning everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be on the winning side. It's a strange thing, being the guy who's fine while the people who taught you aren't. I don't have an answer for that.

headlineQuote: It's a strange thing, being the guy who's fine while the people who taught you aren't.
portrait: Hassan Rahman is 27, the senior dozer operator and earthworks crew lead at an open-pit lithium mine, where he already runs a dozer remotely for half his shifts. He uses AI every day, runs a growing weekend drone surveying business and has strong savings and investments. He is calm and even excited in the milder pictures, anxious when AGI arrives in two years and his habit of staying one step ahead stops working, and calmer again with five or ten years. His answer to AGI is ownership: buying into an autonomous machine fleet and turning his drone work into a business he owns rather than a job he does.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd be scrambling instead of planning.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses to buy their own machines, so big companies don't end up owning everything.
